comparator.name: Philosophy
comparator.sourceNotes: The 2026–27 programme-specific regulations and cohort page control the standard 180 EC full-time Philosophy bachelor, taught in Dutch with some English. The major comprises 60 EC of first-year courses, 30 EC in one advanced package, 15 EC of disciplinary breadth, a 7.5 EC preparation seminar and a 7.5 EC thesis. The remaining 60 EC includes a coherent 30 EC package and 30 EC of open choices, with at least 15 EC at level 2 or 3. The four advanced package courses plus seminar and thesis satisfy the 45 EC level-3 major minimum. The 2026 cohort is expected to take the odd-year History of Political Philosophy when it reaches the advanced package in 2027–28, based on the published alternation. The current cohort page and regulations take precedence over the recruitment page’s bridging-package description.
components: This course alternates with History of Ethics. Utrecht lists History of Political Philosophy for academic years starting in an odd calendar year, which includes 2027–28.
Students complete at least 22.5 EC at level 3 before beginning the graduation sequence. The seminar prepares the thesis in the following block.
This example uses the 7.5 EC thesis. The 15 EC research project requires agreement with the programme coordinator and uses 7.5 EC of open elective space.

routeSelection.basis: The EER requires one of three 30-EC deepening packages and lists Ethics and Politics first. No target-specific evidence distinguishes a student's choice, so the first-listed package is used as a neutral tie-break before any UCR comparison. This route choice instantiates the comparator only; all three official directions remain separately assessed as programme-interest candidates.

core: History of philosophical ideas from antiquity through modern and continental traditions
Ethics, moral responsibility, political power, justice and social philosophy
Knowledge, reality, mind, language, metaphysics and philosophy of science
Logic, philosophical argumentation, close reading, writing and independent research
Philosophical anthropology, human nature, agency, identity and the self
Using philosophy to interpret contemporary social, scientific, technological and artistic problems
adjacent: Ethics and politics as a focused direction in normative judgment, justice and institutions
Language, mind and world as a focused direction in meaning, cognition and reality
What is the human being? as a focused direction in philosophical anthropology and human nature
questions: How do philosophical ideas shape political justice?
How should identity and marginalisation be understood?
How do modern philosophers interpret art?

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

alternatives.label: Philosophy, argument and historical perspectives
alternatives.concept: Study ethics, the mind, free will and political philosophy alongside formal logic and persuasive argument. History, archaeology and literature add ways to examine how ideas about identity, authority and agency develop across cultures and periods.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum combines all five available UCR philosophy courses with political philosophy, logic, rhetoric, historical context and interpretive humanities, so its defining feature is breadth across philosophical questions, argument and historical perspectives.
progression: The plan has six four-course semesters, Personal & Professional Development in Year 1 and 8 courses at level 300. The current workbook confirms each planned offering and earlier formal prerequisite.

alternatives.label: Ethics, politics, justice and institutions
alternatives.concept: Explore moral responsibility, rights and political authority through ethics and political philosophy. Law, politics and social theory provide ways to examine how those questions arise in courts, governments and public debate.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed programme is dominated by ethics and political philosophy, human-rights and public-law study, political institutions, social theory, conflict and argumentative communication; the label names those sustained priorities rather than the external package alone.
alternatives.distinctness: This route gives more sustained attention to rights, political authority and the operation of institutions through public law, comparative politics and social theory.
progression: The plan has six four-course semesters, Personal & Professional Development in Year 1 and 8 courses at level 300. The current workbook confirms each planned offering and earlier formal prerequisite.

alternatives.label: Mind, language, cognition and artificial intelligence
alternatives.concept: Explore consciousness, identity, meaning and agency through philosophy, psycholinguistics and cognitive science. Logic and machine learning add formal and computational tools, while AI ethics examines questions about responsibility and moral status.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum clusters philosophy of mind, emotion and self with psycholinguistics, cognition, brain and behaviour, logic, meaning, machine learning and AI ethics; the final label states that interdisciplinary centre of gravity explicitly.
alternatives.distinctness: This route gives more sustained attention to language processing, consciousness and agency through cognitive neuroscience, experimental psychology and machine learning.
progression: The plan has six four-course semesters, Personal & Professional Development in Year 1 and 7 courses at level 300. The current workbook confirms each planned offering and earlier formal prerequisite.

Uses close reading across periods to strengthen interpretation of major texts and ideas.

Examines philosophical foundations and legal expression of human rights.
Compares world myths and intellectual traditions as material for intercultural reflection.
Examines how linguistic style shapes meaning and argumentative force.
Tests political theories, norms and explanatory arguments in international relations.

Provides qualitative interpretive methods for investigating contemporary social questions.
Investigates free will, time, agency and the self.
Examines political institutions, authority and choices in European governance.
Connects ancient democracy, heritage and contested political interpretation.
Studies persuasive framing, cognitive shortcuts and ethical influence.
Examines emotion, rationality and human experience as philosophy of mind.
Examines Indigenous-centred histories, colonial knowledge and marginalised perspectives.
Uses structural violence, peacebuilding and transitional justice to study how societies respond to conflict.
Compares humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural minority and psychoanalytic approaches to interpretation through a research project.
Introduces law, social order and competing conceptions of justice.
Examines collective action, environmental justice and marginalisation.
Provides comparative frameworks for political institutions and power.
Studies responsibility, punishment and justice through criminal law.
Uses hegemony, public spheres, civil society and decolonial critique to investigate how power and solidarity operate in public life.
Compares constitutional arrangements, rights and distributions of political authority.
Examines the legal and institutional foundations of European political order.
Adds major modern social theories for analysing institutions and social change.
Uses historical analysis of gender, intersectionality and sexuality to investigate how societies construct and contest identities.
Complements philosophical writing with question formulation, critical source evaluation and a substantial historical research paper.
Applies ethical reasoning to artificial intelligence, agency and responsibility.
Introduces brain, behaviour and cognition as empirical perspectives on mind and human nature.
Adds empirical context to questions about animal minds and consciousness through comparative nervous systems, behaviour and sentience.
Provides computational foundations for examining artificial systems and representation.
Develops experimental and statistical methods for claims about mind and behaviour.
Develops close reading of narrative, perspective and figurative language as tools for interpreting how texts produce meaning.
Studies sensory processing and goal-directed behaviour using cognitive neuroscience and neuropsychology.
Examines the relation between language processing, cognition and the brain.
Examines how persons think and act in social contexts.
Studies advanced cognition and higher-order mental functions.
Provides computational methods for prediction, classification and evaluation that support inquiry into artificial learning.
Adds systematic review, bias assessment and meta-analysis to the study of psychological evidence.

Both courses examine major ethical theories and ask what makes actions right or wrong.
Both courses examine political power, freedom and justice. Utrecht also develops social philosophy through intensive writing.
Utrecht builds on introductory ethics to study rights, duties, consent and moral equality.
Utrecht asks whether moral claims can be objectively true and how moral knowledge is possible.
Utrecht studies global justice through political philosophy, including migration, trade and distribution of resources.

Both courses examine the mind–body problem and competing accounts of consciousness and mental life.
Utrecht studies scepticism, what counts as knowledge and how to distinguish science from pseudoscience.
Both courses use formal logic to assess arguments. Utrecht also introduces questions about linguistic meaning.
Utrecht studies the aims and methods of philosophy and develops a proposal for the thesis.

selection.assessment: The closest match covers the broad cross-subdisciplinary Philosophy core. The first two official deepening-package directions, Ethics and Politics and Language, Mind and World, each produce a coherent and materially distinct 24-course UCR curriculum and are included as alternatives 2 and 3. The remaining official What Is the Human Being? direction is independently coherent and supported by philosophical anthropology, continental philosophy and identity interests, but the production contract permits at most three UCR alternatives; it is therefore recorded as maximum-reached rather than mischaracterised as incoherent or infeasible.

notes.text: UCR offers substantial study of ethics, political philosophy, the mind and agency. Utrecht devotes more of the degree to philosophy, including a chronological history sequence, advanced study in one philosophical area and a required philosophy thesis.

audience.programmeDescription: Utrecht’s Philosophy bachelor studies questions about knowledge, reality, moral responsibility and political justice. Students develop philosophical arguments, read texts from different periods and choose an advanced package. This example follows Ethics and Politics.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR options share study of ethics and the philosophy of mind. They differ in their emphasis on historical interpretation, rights and public institutions, or cognition and AI. Utrecht offers a more extensive philosophy curriculum and requires a philosophy thesis.
